content: The preferred treatment regimen for empiric antimicrobial therapy in encephalitis is intravenous acyclovir at a dose of 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for a duration of 14 to 21 days. For patients with agammaglobulinemia, pathogens such as enteroviruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae should be considered. In neonates, common pathogens include herpes simplex virus type 2, cytomegalovirus, rubella virus, Listeria monocytogenes, Treponema pallidum, and Toxoplasma gondii. In infants and children, pathogens such as Eastern equine encephalitis virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, Murray Valley encephalitis virus, influenza virus, and La Crosse virus are more likely. In elderly individuals, pathogens such as Eastern equine encephalitis virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), and Listeria monocytogenes are of concern. Animal contact can also guide pathogen considerations: Bats are associated with rabies virus and Nipah virus. Birds may transmit West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis virus, Western equine encephalitis virus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, Murray Valley encephalitis virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and Cryptococcus neoformans (via bird droppings). Cats are linked to rabies virus, Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella henselae, and Toxoplasma gondii. Dogs are associated with rabies virus. Horses may transmit Eastern equine encephalitis virus, Western equine encephalitis virus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, and Hendra virus. Old World primates are linked to B virus. Raccoons may transmit rabies virus and Baylisascaris procyonis. Rodents are associated with Eastern equine encephalitis virus (in South America), Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, tickborne encephalitis virus, Powassan virus (woodchucks), La Crosse virus (chipmunks and squirrels), and Bartonella quintana. Sheep and goats are linked to Coxiella burnetii. Skunks may transmit rabies virus. Swine are associated with Japanese encephalitis virus and Nipah virus. White-tailed deer are linked to Borrelia burgdorferi. In immunocompromised individuals, pathogens such as varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, West Nile virus, HIV, JC virus, Listeria monocytogenes, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans, Coccidioides species, Histoplasma capsulatum, and Toxoplasma gondii should be considered. Ingestion of raw or undercooked meat is associated with Toxoplasma gondii. Consumption of raw meat, fish, or reptiles may lead to infections with Gnathostoma species. Unpasteurized milk is linked to tickborne encephalitis virus, Listeria monocytogenes, and Coxiella burnetii. Insect contact is another important consideration: Mosquitoes may transmit Eastern equine encephalitis virus, Western equine encephalitis virus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, Murray Valley encephalitis virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, La Crosse virus, and Plasmodium falciparum. Sandflies are associated with Bartonella bacilliformis. Ticks may transmit tickborne encephalitis virus, Powassan virus, Rickettsia rickettsii, Ehrlichia chaffeensis, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Coxiella burnetii (rarely), and Borrelia burgdorferi. Tsetse flies are linked to Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense. Occupational exposures can also guide pathogen considerations: Animal exposure is associated with rabies virus, Coxiella burnetii, and Bartonella species. Exposure to horses is linked to Hendra virus. Exposure to Old World primates is associated with B virus. Laboratory workers may encounter West Nile virus, HIV, Coxiella burnetii, and Coccidioides species. Physicians and healthcare workers are at risk for varicella-zoster virus, HIV, influenza virus, measles virus, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Veterinarians may encounter rabies virus, Bartonella species, and Coxiella burnetii. Person-to-person transmission is possible with herpes simplex virus (neonatal), varicella-zoster virus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (rare), poliovirus, non-polio enteroviruses, measles virus, Nipah virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, Epstein-Barr virus, human herpesvirus 6, B virus, West Nile virus (via transfusion, transplantation, or breastfeeding), HIV, rabies virus (via transplantation), influenza virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Treponema pallidum. Recent vaccination may lead to acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Recreational activities such as camping or hunting may expose individuals to mosquitoand tickborne pathogens. Sexual contact is associated with HIV and Treponema pallidum. Spelunking is linked to rabies virus and Histoplasma capsulatum. Swimming may expose individuals to enteroviruses and Naegleria fowleri. Seasonal patterns are also relevant: Late summer and early fall are associated with mosquitoand tickborne pathogens, as well as enteroviruses. Winter is linked to influenza virus. Transmission through transfusion or transplantation may involve cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, West Nile virus, HIV, tickborne encephalitis virus, rabies virus, iatrogenic CJD, Treponema pallidum, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Rickettsia rickettsii, Cryptococcus neoformans, Coccidioides species, Histoplasma capsulatum, and Toxoplasma gondii. Travel history is critical: In Africa, consider rabies virus, West Nile virus, Plasmodium falciparum, Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense. In Australia, pathogens include Murray Valley encephalitis virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and Hendra virus. In Central America, consider rabies virus, Eastern equine encephalitis virus, Western equine encephalitis virus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, Rickettsia rickettsii, Plasmodium falciparum, and Taenia solium. In Europe, pathogens include West Nile virus, tickborne encephalitis virus, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and Borrelia burgdorferi. In India and Nepal, consider rabies virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and Plasmodium falciparum. In the Middle East, pathogens include West Nile virus and Plasmodium falciparum. In Russia, tickborne encephalitis virus is a concern. In South America, consider rabies virus, Eastern equine encephalitis virus, Western equine encephalitis virus, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, Rickettsia rickettsii, Bartonella bacilliformis (in the Andes), Plasmodium falciparum, and Taenia solium. In Southeast Asia, China, and the Pacific Rim, pathogens include Japanese encephalitis virus, tickborne encephalitis virus, Nipah virus, Plasmodium falciparum, Gnathostoma species, and Taenia solium. Unvaccinated individuals are at risk for varicella-zoster virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, poliovirus, measles virus, mumps virus, and rubella virus. Specific clinical findings can guide diagnosis: Hepatitis may indicate Coxiella burnetii. Lymphadenopathy is associated with HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, measles virus, rubella virus, West Nile virus, Treponema pallidum, Bartonella species, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Toxoplasma gondii, and Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. Parotitis is linked to mumps virus. Rash may indicate varicella-zoster virus, B virus, human herpesvirus 6, West Nile virus, rubella virus, enteroviruses, HIV, Rickettsia rickettsii, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Borrelia burgdorferi, Treponema pallidum, Ehrlichia chaffeensis, and Anaplasma phagocytophilum. Respiratory findings may suggest Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, Nipah virus, Hendra virus, influenza virus, adenovirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Coxiella burnetii, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, or Histoplasma capsulatum. Retinitis is associated with cytomegalovirus, West Nile virus, Bartonella henselae, and Treponema pallidum. Urinary symptoms may indicate St. Louis encephalitis virus. Neurologic findings include: Cerebellar ataxia, which may be caused by varicella-zoster virus (in children), Epstein-Barr virus, mumps virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, Tropheryma whipplei, and Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. Cranial nerve abnormalities, which may be linked to herpes simplex virus, Epstein-Barr virus, Listeria monocytogenes, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi, Tropheryma whipplei, Cryptococcus neoformans, Coccidioides species, and Histoplasma capsulatum. Dementia, which may be caused by HIV, human transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (sCJD and vCJD), measles virus (subacute sclerosing panencephalitis), Treponema pallidum, and Tropheryma whipplei. Myorhythmia (oculomasticatory) is associated with Tropheryma whipplei. Parkinsonism may be caused by Japanese encephalitis virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, Nipah virus, Toxoplasma gondii, and Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. Poliomyelitis-like flaccid paralysis is linked to Japanese encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, tickborne encephalitis virus, enteroviruses (e.g., enterovirus-71, coxsackieviruses), and poliovirus. Rhombencephalitis may be caused by herpes simplex virus, West Nile virus, enterovirus-71, and Listeria monocytogenes. Pathogen-directed antimicrobial therapy includes: For adenovirus: supportive care. For B virus (herpes B virus): Established disease: Valacyclovir 1,000 mg orally three times daily or Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for at least 14 days until neurologic symptoms resolve, followed by indefinite oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily or valacyclovir 1 g three times daily. Alternative: Acyclovir 15 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for at least 14 days until neurologic symptoms resolve, followed by indefinite oral acyclovir or valacyclovir. Prophylaxis after bite or scratch: Valacyclovir 1,000 mg orally three times daily. For cytomegalovirus (CMV): Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 14–21 days, followed by 5 mg/kg IV daily for maintenance, or Foscarnet 90 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 14–21 days, followed by 90–120 mg/kg IV daily for maintenance. For Eastern equine encephalitis virus: supportive care. For Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): supportive care, with or without corticosteroids. For Hendra virus: supportive care. For HSV-1 and HSV-2: Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 14–21 days. For neonates, Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 21 days. For human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6): Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 14–21 days, followed by 5 mg/kg IV daily for maintenance, or Foscarnet 90 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 14–21 days, followed by 90–120 mg/kg IV daily for maintenance. For HIV: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). For influenza virus: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily. For Japanese encephalitis virus: supportive care. For JC virus: reversal or control of immunosuppression, or HAART in AIDS patients. For La Crosse virus: supportive care. For measles virus: Ribavirin for life-threatening disease. For subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE): intrathecal Ribavirin. For mumps virus: supportive care. For Murray Valley encephalitis virus: supportive care. For Nipah virus: supportive care, with Ribavirin as an alternative. For non-polio enteroviruses: supportive care. For poliovirus: supportive care. For Powassan virus: supportive care. For rabies virus: supportive care. For rubella virus: supportive care.
